title: Can Writing More Make Sense in Classes like Phys Ed, Band, or Computer Science? -science
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Following up on his call for daily "provisional writing," Stuart addresses skeptics by arguing that every class — not just English or history — exists to help students master something they otherwise wouldn't, and that writing belongs in a class only insofar as it serves that class's specific kind of mastery. He works through concrete, low-lift examples for physical education (a weekly fitness/goal-setting log), band (a short daily musician's log with reflective prompts), and computer science (periodic five-minute free-writes about problem-solving), each designed to fit within classes where time is scarce. He closes by naming three properties of writing that make it broadly useful across disciplines: it focuses the mind, clarifies muddy thinking, and makes visible to both student and teacher what would otherwise stay invisible. The piece functions as a practical rebuttal to the idea that writing-across-the-curriculum is only for "writing" subjects.
points: Stuart's organizing principle — "for writing to make sense in a given class, the writing must somehow be contributing toward that class' essential purpose" — reframes writing-across-the-curriculum as a mastery question rather than a literacy mandate.
He proposes low-time-cost formats (a weekly phys-ed fitness log, a short daily band-practice log, periodic CS free-writes) that respect how little slack time non-ELA classes actually have.
The biology/photosynthesis example illustrates his core diagnostic claim: verbal nods of recognition from a class mask gaps that two minutes of academic-vocabulary free-writing reveals immediately.

He names three transferable properties of writing — focusing the mind, clarifying muddy thinking, and making the invisible visible — as the real argument for why writing belongs in every discipline, not just English.
quotes: Classes (and schools) exist to promote the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them to master things they otherwise wouldn't.

And this then brings us to a core principle for deciding when and how to incorporate writing into a class. For writing to make sense in a given class, the writing must somehow be contributing toward that class' essential purpose.

Doesn't it seem brilliant to have students keeping at least a weekly log of their physical activity? Of fitness goal-setting? Of reflecting on how eating or sleeping patterns influence their performance in class?
In band, I'd picture something similar. In band, time is also very precious. Class size can be huge.
Writing focuses the mind. I've yet to figure out how to both write and daydream.

Writing clarifies muddy thinking. This is part of why the book writing process is such a necessary misery for me — it forces me to face the parts of my thinking that, apart from writing, would always just be safely fuzzy in the clouds of my mind.

If I'm a biology teacher and I ask my students verbally, "You all remember photosynthesis from last unit, right?" I'm likely to get many nods. But if I instead ask my students to spend two minutes free-writing about photosynthesis in their spiral notebooks using as many academic vocabulary words as they can, now I (and they) KNOW whether they remember it or not.
